surface_forms: la seule personne qui avait assez vécu auprès de Vinteuil

appraisal_events.evidence: Beside the septet the sonata and the other works are «que de timides essais, délicieux mais bien frêles, auprès du chef-d'œuvre triomphal et complet»; Vinteuil's accent is «une preuve de l'existence irréductiblement individuelle de l'âme», his colours unimitable by «toutes les règles du monde», his creative fury likened to «Michel-Ange attaché à son échelle» at the Sistine ceiling, and his art, like Elstir's, is what lets us «voir l'univers avec les yeux d'un autre».
appraisal_events.explanation: The passage's central movement is an unqualified narratorial exaltation of Vinteuil, raised from the sad little Combray bourgeois to a creator whose work is the proof that something other than the void exists.

appraisal_events.evidence: Alone able to read the «indéchiffrables notations», she spent years «à débrouiller le grimoire laissé par Vinteuil», compared to a chemist's illegible notebooks, and thereby «eut la consolation d'assurer au musicien dont elle avait assombri les dernières années une gloire immortelle et compensatrice»; the carnal disorder of Montjouvain has «fait place à la flamme d'une amitié haute et pure», and it is «grâce à elle» that the narrator receives the call he will never stop hearing.
appraisal_events.explanation: The woman of the Montjouvain profanation is explicitly redeemed by her labour, and the same act posthumously secures Vinteuil the glory the world would otherwise never have known.

appraisal_events.evidence: «Mlle Vinteuil n'avait agi que par sadisme, ce qui ne l'excusait pas, mais j'eus plus tard une certaine douceur à le penser» — her profanation is re-read as «une simulation de méchanceté», «maladif, de la folie, et pas la vraie et joyeuse méchanceté qu'elle aurait voulue», and the narrator wishes he could restore «entre elle et le souvenir de son père une communication assez douce»; her adoration of her father is called «la condition même du sacrilège».
appraisal_events.explanation: The narration revisits and materially softens its verdict on her, converting the sacrilege from wickedness into illness without pretending to absolve her.

appraisal_events.evidence: During the refreshments he hails the footmen — «Avez-vous reçu mon pneumatique ? Viendrez-vous ?» — with the grand seigneur's freedom and «la rouerie du coupable qui croit que ce dont on fait étalage est par cela même jugé innocent»; but «ses habiletés tournaient contre le baron, car on trouvait extraordinaires ses amabilités si intimes et ses pneumatiques à des valets de pied», the servants themselves being «moins flattés que gênés pour leurs camarades».
appraisal_events.explanation: His attempt to disarm suspicion by display is registered by the room as exactly what he meant to conceal, and even the servants are embarrassed; the narration endorses the company's reading.

status_effects.explanation: The narration's verdict on him rises to the highest possible: an original of the rank of the greatest, whose work outranks everything previously known of him.
Years of patience, intelligence and respect turn the accomplice of Montjouvain into the person to whom the revelation of Vinteuil's work is owed.

Distinct from the narrator's private verdict: through the deciphering, his reputation in the world is transformed — «une gloire immortelle et compensatrice», with the later public declaring his last works his deepest.
Her standing in the narration improves: the sacrilege is reinterpreted as simulated, pathological wickedness rooted in the very cult of her father, and the narrator turns toward pity.
A witnessed loss: the assembled company finds his intimacies with footmen extraordinary, so the display that was meant to protect him lowers him instead.

ambiguities: The re-judgment of Mlle Vinteuil is expressly double — «ce qui ne l'excusait pas» stands beside the narrator's wish to console her — so the softening is a mitigation of guilt rather than an acquittal.
